learningObjectives: Explain at a high level what quantum computing is.
Distinguish a classical bit from a qubit.
Identify |0⟩ and |1⟩ as the computational basis states.
Recognize |ψ⟩ as notation for a quantum state.
Understand at an introductory level that quantum computing manipulates quantum states using quantum gates and circuits.
Recognize that later lessons will explain superposition, measurement, amplitudes, phase, and gates in greater depth.

Concept of quantum gates as state transformations

scenes.title: What Is a Classical Bit?

narration.speaker: QUALUTION Narrator
narration.text: At the heart of every classical device is the bit—the basic unit of binary information. A classical bit is strictly deterministic: it can only ever be in one state at any moment: 0 OR 1. To evaluate multiple possibilities, classical computers must process them sequentially, one state at a time.

scenes.title: Introducing the Qubit

narration.speaker: QUALUTION Narrator
narration.text: In quantum computing, the fundamental unit of information is called a qubit. Just like classical bits, a qubit can be measured as 0 or 1, which we write using Dirac notation as |0⟩ and |1⟩. These are known as the computational basis states, and they form the foundation of everything we build.

scenes.title: The Quantum State (|ψ⟩)

narration.speaker: QUALUTION Narrator
narration.text: To describe where a qubit is at any given moment, we write its quantum state as |ψ⟩. Mathematically, we express this state as a combination of basis states: |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩. Here, alpha and beta are numbers called probability amplitudes. We will explore their exact meaning in dedicated upcoming lessons.

scenes.title: Why Quantum States Are Special

narration.speaker: QUALUTION Narrator
narration.text: Unlike a classical bit that is locked to a single binary value, a quantum state contains a richer geometric structure. This hidden structure allows quantum computers to process information using principles like superposition, phase, and interference.

captions.text: Unlike a classical bit locked to a single value, a quantum state contains a richer geometric structure.

scenes.title: Quantum Gates: The Operations

narration.speaker: QUALUTION Narrator
narration.text: Just as classical computers use logic gates like AND and NOT, quantum computers use quantum gates. A quantum gate is an operation that transforms an input quantum state into a new output state. Gates like X, H, and Z are the primary building blocks you will use to construct quantum algorithms.

scenes.title: The Quantum Circuit

narration.speaker: QUALUTION Narrator
narration.text: When we connect quantum gates along a timeline, we create a quantum circuit. Each horizontal line represents a qubit wire, and gates are applied sequentially from left to right. At the end of the circuit, measurement converts the final quantum state into readable classical bits.

scenes.title: What Makes Quantum Computing Different?

narration.speaker: QUALUTION Narrator
narration.text: Classical computers solve problems using discrete bits and boolean logic gates. Quantum computers operate on quantum states, using quantum gates to explore computational spaces in entirely new ways.

captions.text: Classical computers solve problems using discrete bits and boolean logic gates.
